questions.q: What does .option("mergeSchema", "true") do on a write?
options: Disables schema enforcement entirely for all future writes
Deliberately widens the table's schema to include a genuinely new column, instead of rejecting the mismatch
Deletes any existing rows that don't match the new schema
Converts the table from Delta back to plain Parquet
questions.explain: Existing rows get the new column filled with null, since they genuinely have no value for it.

questions.q: Does mergeSchema allow changing an existing column's type from double to string?
options: No — that's a lossy type change and is still rejected as a real error, on purpose
Yes, mergeSchema allows any type change without restriction
Only when using the CLI, never through PySpark
Only if the column has no existing data in it
questions.explain: Schema evolution is about safely growing a schema additively, not disabling schema enforcement altogether.

questions.q: What does ALTER TABLE trips ADD COLUMN payment_type STRING do, compared to mergeSchema?
options: It deletes the payment_type column if it already exists
It changes the schema directly and immediately, as its own deliberate step, independent of any particular write
It has the exact same effect and timing as mergeSchema, with no real difference
It only works on temporary views, never persistent Delta tables
questions.explain: Real production pipelines often prefer this explicit, planned migration over an implicit change from a write's flag.

questions.q: Why is schema evolution described as a common event rather than an edge case?
options: Schemas never actually need to change in real production systems
It's actually extremely rare and mostly a theoretical concern
Schema evolution only matters for test/development tables, never production
Real pipelines evolve — a source system adds a field, or a business question needs a new column that didn't exist before
questions.explain: This connects back to Foundations' raw/cleansed/curated zones, which existed partly because data shape genuinely changes over time.

questions.q: What happens to existing rows in a table after a mergeSchema write adds a new column?
options: Existing rows get a default value of 0 or empty string
Existing rows are unaffected and simply lack the new column entirely, causing errors on read
Existing rows are deleted and must be rewritten
Existing rows get the new column filled with null, since they have no value for it
questions.explain: This is the expected, safe behavior for an additive schema change.
